If you have a similar background to me, you’ll expect to be able to write your code using an editor of your choice, arranging it into files containing logically related routines, which you then put into a source code revision management system, like git, perhaps triggering a build and test pipeline on every commit via something like
. This is most likely in the neighbourhood of your current workflow, regardless of which language or platform you’re using, from
Before we get into the practicalities of how you can do this and more, we’ll need a slight diversion into the history of APL and Dyalog in particular [
]. Firstly, APL predates all these workflows and build tools. That in itself isn’t an issue: so does C. But APL wasn’t really conceived as a
tool. During its heyday, middle management and CFOs were slinging APL to generate forecasts and reports, and they

APL as it allowed them to essentially perform tasks that up until then had been in the realm of specialist “batch processing” on the company mainframe. It essentially occupied the niche which is now dominated by Microsoft Excel.

This influenced all APL vendors, including Dyalog. Commercial APL systems are fully integrated application stacks that make it seductively convenient to package up your work as binary workspaces that can be easily distributed to other APL users without ever having to “leave” the confines of the stack itself. Dyalog’s tooling and development philosophy supports this world view, as that is what many of its customers expect: professional Dyalog developers working for billion-dollar financial institutions will be of the opinion that you can pry their binary workspaces from their cold, dead hands. You can build fully-fledged, GUI-driven applications integrating deeply with code bases written in .NET.

Yet, for you, the newcomer, this approach will probably feel a bit alien. Dyalog obviously understand this, and they’re walking the tightrope of both delivering what their current paying, long-term customers need, but also a keen eye on what
users and potential customers might be looking to. Morten Kromberg, Dyalog CTO, wrote a
chat room, but also touching on some of Dyalog’s challenges when dealing with this dichotomy.

There are a couple of other topics that I should possibly also explain my views on, such as the dilemma of whether APL is a Notation or a Programming Language, and why Dyalog APL is not open source, but this post is very long already. Depending on the response I get to this post, I may return to that in the future. --
Fortunately, and for the avoidance of any doubt, you can

work with modern Dyalog (I’m using version 21.0 at the time of writing this) in a pretty similar way to what you expect, but it requires a little bit of setup to get right, and is not quite there “out of the box” at the time of writing. However, at the time of
some of the kinks may well have been ironed out: better support for Dyalog as a scripting engine, and working with code-as-text is a priority for Dyalog right now.
We mentioned workspaces when we talked about namespaces earlier. Let’s return to take another look at them and then at the
tool that allows you to keep your code in text files that can be versioned.
Source Code Management with GitHub and APL

, you’ll see no “Save as..” in the menu, and your OS’s default key binding for “Save” does nothing. You might have figured out how to enter multi-line functions, and how to “fix” (somewhere between “save” and “compile”) them. Yet, when you “fix” a function, where does it go?

At no point were you asked for a file name. Again, the Excel analogy might help to clarify. Think of a cell containing a formula in Excel -- you’re not expecting to “save” the formula out to a separate file. Instead, the formula becomes an integral part of the sheet or workbook. We can think of Dyalog workspaces as analogous to Excel workbooks: a snapshot of values and the logic to manipulate them. It has the nice feature that if you distribute a workspace, you can be sure that users of that workspace sees exactly what you intended: it’s an exact snapshot.

command. As you might expect, the workspace concept is deeply engrained in Dyalog and it comes with rich, sophisticated, thoroughly battle-tested functionality -- all of which is overkill for our needs right now. If you want to explore this further, Legrand’s book,

is a Dyalog library that can be used to set up synchronisation between a directory of text files containing APL source code, and namespaces in your current workspace. As you may recall from the chapter on

, one way to think of them is as a grouping mechanism akin to a module or class. Recent Dyalog versions come with Link bundled, but it’s under active development and you can always install the latest version from the above link.

The Link concept is pretty intuitive: a Linked directory becomes a namespace, and all its content loaded. If you make a change to a file using an external tool or editor, that change will be reflected inside Dyalog, and if you make a change to the namespace inside Dyalog, these changes are reflected on disk. This means that you can write APL code in Emacs or VS Code, and have your Dyalog session see any changes you make. And -- of course -- now you can put your code in github with all that this entails in terms of your workflow.

Our functions have clearly been loaded. Let’s see if they work, shall we?
That works really well so far. Any change we make in

namespace will be reflected on disk, including new functions, or modifications of existing. Bi-directional sync is really what we want, so that if the files change on disk -- for example if you’re editing a function with an external editor, that change will be picked up by the interpreter. This works out of the box on Windows, but for Linux and macOS, for Dyalog v21, you will first need to install
, as the file system watcher for Link relies on .NET. If you’re an
user of Dyalog APL, you’re out of luck, as .NET isn’t available for AIX.

If you -- as a linux or macOS user -- are thinking “Why the hell should I have to install a completely separate development toolchain I have zero interest in just so that Dyalog APL can see if I changed a file?”, well, it’s a fair point. Picking up file system change notifications from the OS in a platform independent way is simple in .NET and not simple in any other way that is easily integrated with Dyalog APL. If you think of .NET as Dyalog’s core extension mechanism (we’ve deemed that out of scope for this book), perhaps you can see why Dyalog went down this route. Dyalog’s longer term plans have always been to let the interpreter eventually take over Link’s job.

The other thing is that when you’re working this way, you’ll need to keep each function, namespace, class, or operator in its own separate file, and they all have their separate file extensions, which if you’re anything like me is quite a fine granularity, especially since APL functions tend to be pretty short. If Dyalog’s gazillion different file extensions rub up wrongly against your core sensibilities, well, that is fair cop, too.
Finally, and most importantly, Link is NOT an application
mechanism, no matter how much it can be dressed up as one.

distribute a system to end user that relies on Link to load code into a workspace. Bad things will eventually happen. Link is intended as a tool for the development workflow. Don’t use Link to simulate the import functionality you wish that Dyalog had.
Another thing is that Links file system notification system sometimes gets overwhelmed by too many rapid changes. If you have a linked directory of many thousands of files and you suddenly do a
to a different branch, the resulting state in the interpreter may be ... ill-defined. Prefer to unlink before the switch, and then re-link.

executable allows you to execute a text file containing APL code, top to bottom, with function definitions and all, from the command-line. This means that with this approach you can use Dyalog for ‘quick and dirty’ scripts where you otherwise would have reached for Python, and that you can easily share code as files, or via a github gist and have other people run it.

For example, I created the following file:

#!/usr/bin/env dyalogscript
⍝ Draw the shortest way through an ASCII maze: '#' is wall, anything else is open.
⍝ Mazes from https://www.dcode.fr/maze-generator

⎕IO←0
'span' 'stpath'⎕CY'dfns'

Graph ← {                                     ⍝ ⍵:open-cell mask → dfns adjacency list
    id ← (⍴⍵)⍴(+\,⍵)×,⍵                       ⍝ number the openings 1…n, walls stay 0
    nb ← ↑,¨(0⍪¯1 0↓id)(0,0 ¯1↓id)((0 1↓id),0)((1 0↓id)⍪0)   ⍝ up, left, right, down
    {¯1+⍵/⍨0≠⍵}¨↓⍉nb[;⍸,⍵]                   ⍝ per opening: the neighbours that exist
}

Ends ← {                                      ⍝ ⍵:maze → coordinates of start and goal
    2=≢m←⍸~⍵∊'#.': m                          ⍝ the two lettered squares if marked…
    c[0,¯1+≢c←⍸~'#'=⍵]                        ⍝ …otherwise first and last opening
}

Solve ← {                                     ⍝ ⍵:maze → maze with the path drawn on
    cells ← ⍸open←~'#'=⍵                      ⍝ node k is the k'th opening, row-major
    (start goal) ← cells⍳Ends ⍵
    '⎕'@(cells[((Graph open)span start)stpath goal])⊢⍵
}

argv ← 2⎕NQ'.' 'GetCommandLineArgs'
file ← ⊃(1↓argv),⊂(⊃⎕NPARTS⊃argv),'maze-small.txt'   ⍝ default: next to the script

⎕ ← Solve↑⊃⎕NGET file 1

is the most widely deployed IDE in the world. Statistically speaking, as a software developer, you probably have it installed on the machine you’re reading this on. Dyalog has an unofficial

, and it pulls off an impressive feat: it manages to fit Dyalog APL into the standard VS Code workflow in terms of tracing, file handling etc, without sacrificing the dynamic nature of the session. It has a session pane that maintains a persistent connection to a running Dyalog APL session, and for AI fans, this can be shared with whatever LLM agent which happens to be en vogue (a moving goal post).
The interesting thing is that all of that was achieved without any changes to the Dyalog APL interpreter itself. Here are a couple of screnshots of this in action:
I’ve started the interpreter ‘inside’ VS Code by clicking the
button in the APL window, and typed the convenience command
to load up the contents of the open folder. Any modifications I make to files will be picked up by the interpreter via Link.
The extension has full DAP support, too, meaning that you can take advantage of VS Code’s normal debugger tools to trace through your Dyalog APL code:
Many -- maybe even most -- software projects today tend to be heterogeneous: perhaps your backends are written in Go, speaking
, exposing a json-http API, picked up by a javascript

. Integrating Dyalog APL components in such architectures works well, and being able to stay in VS Code for all parts of the application architecture feels more ergonomic perhaps than switching out to a separate toolchain for the Dyalog bits.
The VS Code extension is still young, but if you’re working in a mixed environment, it will probably fit the bill.
